bibliography.abstract: Traffic-related air pollution is a major contributor to respiratory and cardiovascular disease, and travel time disproportionately drives daily exposure. Conventional routing algorithms minimize time or distance, ignoring street-level pollutant variability and leaving travelers exposed to avoidable risk. We develop a bi-objective routing framework that couples a high-resolution AERMOD-based PM2.5 dispersion surface with a shortest-path algorithm. The algorithm uses a deterministic, gradient-based weight-update scheme to enumerate Pareto-optimal paths along the time-exposure frontier. We apply the framework to 790,000 origin-destination pairs on New York City's road network, covering 1.48 million daily commuters. Link-level concentrations differed by a factor of two or more between adjacent parallel streets. Exposure-aware routes reduced cumulative exposure by about 38% at a median travel time increase of about 28%. The algorithm ran in 30 milliseconds per query and recovered more frontier paths than uniform weight sampling (4.5 vs. 2.4). These results show that exposure-aware routing is computationally practical at metropolitan scale and suitable for real-time navigation and infrastructure planning.

bibliography.title: Modeling the Travel Time-Pollution Exposure Trade-off in Urban Route Choice

en.what: A bi-objective routing framework couples high-resolution AERMOD PM2.5 dispersion modeling with a gradient-based shortest-path algorithm to map Pareto-optimal trade-offs between travel time and pollution exposure. Applied across 790,000 origin-destination pairs and 1.48 million daily commuters in New York City, exposure-aware routes reduced cumulative PM2.5 exposure by roughly 38% while incurring a median travel time penalty of about 28%. The algorithm executes in 30 milliseconds per query and identifies an average of 4.5 frontier paths compared to 2.4 using traditional uniform weight sampling.
en.why: It demonstrates that micro-level pollution variations between adjacent streets can be leveraged for health-optimal navigation without causing severe computational overhead or excessive travel delays at metropolitan scales.
